newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's return to China to benefit HK economy-Lehman.
newsitem.headline: HK's return to China to benefit HK economy-Lehman.

text.p: Hong Kong's reversion to Chinese rule should boost economic growth in the territory and bolster its status as an international financial centre, Lehman Brothers said on Tuesday.

"We will see greater economic integration between China and Hong Kong," Lehman Brothers Asia chief economist Miron Mushkat told a Lehman Brothers seminar. "Capital will be flowing more freely between Hong Kong and China."
The British colony returns to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
Hong Kong's role as a bridge between China and the rest of the world, and also its economy, will grow as the Chinese economy develops, Mushkat said.
"The more China opens up, the more China reforms...the more it needs a middleman like Hong Kong to act as a go-between for China and the rest of the world," he said.
Shanghai cannot supplant Hong Kong as China's key middleman in the medium term because it lacks the skills required for international trade, Mushkat said.

The skills include a good knowledge of English, familiarity with modern business practices, the ability to operate in different cultural and legal environment, and proficiency with complex contractual arrangements, Mushkat said.
"Hong Kong is bi-cultural, bilingual, can operate as an effective bridge between China and the rest of the world," he said.
"Shanghai does not pose a realistic challenge to Hong Kong today," he said. "You don't become an international financial centre just through government design," he said.
"And Shanghai will not become an international financial centre probably in my life time," Mushkat said. "Why not? Because it is not bi-cultural, bilingual."
Also, the supporting industries of international trade are capital- and skill-intensive and not entirely appropriate for a developing country, he said.

But Hong Kong needs to maintain its present legal system and its laissez-faire regulatory regime and stay a market-driven economy in order to maintain its status as an international financial centre, he said.
It also needs to keep corruption and taxation low, safeguard the media's independence, and ensure the effectiveness of its civil service, Mushkat said.
After the handover, Hong Kong will continue to have a strong single-A sovereign risk rating which will be higher than China's, Lehman Brothers Asia managing director Stephen Taran said.
"The transition is not going to have an impact, except a beneficial impact, on the credit quality of Hong Kong as a sovereign risk," he said.
"Foreign investors are increasingly buying the story about Hong Kong being a very strong single-A sovereign credit," he said.
